content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'lost sheep' symbolizes the sinner who has strayed from God — and by extension straying humanity generally — whom God (or Christ the Good Shepherd) actively seeks out, finds, and joyfully restores. The image emphasizes divine initiative in seeking the lost, the value of each individual person to God, and heaven's joy over repentance.","primary_basis":["Luke 15:3-7 (Parable of the Lost Sheep: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one; 'joy in heaven over one sinner who repents')","Matthew 18:12-14 (parallel parable; 'it is not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish')","Isaiah 53:6 ('All we like sheep have gone astray')","Psalm 119:176 ('I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant')","Ezekiel 34:11-16 (God himself will search for his scattered sheep and bring back the strays)","Jeremiah 50:6 ('My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray')","1 Peter 2:25 ('For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls')","Luke 19:10 ('the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The 'lost sheep of the house of Israel': a specific reference to the covenant people Israel as strayed from God, defining the initial scope of Jesus' and the disciples' mission to Israel before the Gentile mission.","basis":["Matthew 10:5-6","Matthew 15:24","Jeremiah 50:6","Ezekiel 34"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Patristic/allegorical cosmic reading: the one lost sheep is fallen humanity (or Adam) while the ninety-nine represent the unfallen angels or heavenly hosts; the Incarnation is the shepherd's descent to retrieve the lost sheep. Found in Irenaeus, Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Alexandria, Hilary, and others.","basis":["Luke 15:3-7 read allegorically","John 10:11-16","patristic homilies and commentaries (e.g., Irenaeus, Against Heresies; Gregory of Nyssa)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The lost sheep as the lapsed or backslidden believer within the church — pastoral application to restoring erring church members rather than evangelizing outsiders, often tied to the Matthew 18 context of 'little ones' in the community.","basis":["Matthew 18:12-14 in its church-discipline context","James 5:19-20","Galatians 6:1"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Identification of the 'lost sheep of the house of Israel' with the literal 'lost ten tribes' and, in British-Israelism/Anglo-Israelism and some related movements, with specific modern nations or peoples.","basis":["Matthew 10:6","Matthew 15:24","2 Kings 17 (exile of the northern tribes)","John 10:16 ('other sheep') as used in these traditions"],"prominence":"rare"},{"meaning":"Sociorhetorical/economic readings in modern scholarship: the parable as a challenge to Pharisaic attitudes toward 'sinners' and table fellowship, focusing on Jesus' defense of eating with outcasts rather than on a doctrine of individual salvation.","basis":["Luke 15:1-2 (narrative frame: Pharisees grumbling about Jesus receiving sinners)","historical-critical parable scholarship (e.g., Jeremias, Bailey)"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a strong, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and evangelical traditions: the lost sheep represents the straying sinner sought and restored by God/Christ. The main interpretive divergence is scope — whether the referent is any sinner, Israel specifically (in Matthew 10 and 15), erring church members, or (allegorically) all fallen humanity versus the angels. These are variations in emphasis rather than contradictions of the core image of straying and divine seeking. Fringe readings (e.g., identifying lost sheep with specific modern nations) exist but are rejected by mainstream scholarship. The related but distinct phrase 'other sheep' (John 10:16) is sometimes conflated with 'lost sheep' in popular and sectarian usage."}
